claim: ENU mutagenesis has been used to generate mutants in Caenorhabditis elegans, flies, zebrafish and mice, but it has never been tried in large model animals.
source: N-ethyl-N-nitrosourea (ENU) mutagenesis is a powerful tool to generate mutants on a large scale efficiently, and to discover genes with novel functions at the whole-genome level in Caenorhabditis elegans, flies, zebrafish and mice, but it has never been tried in large model animals.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that ENU mutagenesis has been used in various model organisms but not in large model animals, establishing the novelty of this study.

claim: A total of 6,770 G1 and 6,800 G3 pigs were screened in this study.
source: A total of 6,770 G1 and 6,800 G3 pigs were screened, 36 dominant and 91 recessive novel pig families with various phenotypes were established.
evidence: The abstract provides specific numbers of pigs screened, which is directly supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 36 dominant and 91 recessive novel pig families with various phenotypes were established.
source: A total of 6,770 G1 and 6,800 G3 pigs were screened, 36 dominant and 91 recessive novel pig families with various phenotypes were established.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of dominant and recessive mutant families identified, supported by screening data in Table 1.

claim: The causative mutations in 10 mutant families were mapped.
source: The causative mutations in 10 mutant families were further mapped.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by Table 2 showing mapping results for 10 mutant lines.

claim: The mutation of SOX10 (R109W) in pig causes inner ear malfunctions and mimics human Mondini dysplasia.
source: As examples, the mutation of SOX10 (R109W) in pig causes inner ear malfunctions and mimics human Mondini dysplasia, and upregulated expression of FBXO32 is associated with congenital splay legs.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by detailed experimental data in Figure 4 showing the SOX10 mutation, hearing loss, and inner ear abnormalities.

claim: Upregulated expression of FBXO32 is associated with congenital splay legs.
source: As examples, the mutation of SOX10 (R109W) in pig causes inner ear malfunctions and mimics human Mondini dysplasia, and upregulated expression of FBXO32 is associated with congenital splay legs.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this association, which is supported by expression data in Figure 5D and 5E showing elevated FBXO32 in affected animals.

claim: Pigs are an important source of meat worldwide and are widely used in biomedical research.
source: Pigs are an important source of meat worldwide and are widely used in biomedical research (Groenen et al., 2012; Prather, 2013; Wernersson et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature establishing the importance of pigs in agriculture and research.

claim: The similarities of organ size, anatomic and physiologic characteristics and genome sequence between pigs and humans stimulated the use of these animals as preferred models of various human diseases.
source: The similarities of organ size, anatomic and physiologic characteristics and genome sequence between pigs and humans stimulated the use of these animals as preferred models of various human diseases and as sources of allogenetic organs for xenotransplantation.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the similarities between pigs and humans.

claim: A draft of pig genome was reported in 2012.
source: Although a draft of pig genome was reported in 2012 and much progress has been made in pig gene identification, mapping and functional analyses, the current knowledge of the pig functional genome remains limited (Brown and Moore, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Brown and Moore, 2012.

claim: The current knowledge of the pig functional genome remains limited.
source: Although a draft of pig genome was reported in 2012 and much progress has been made in pig gene identification, mapping and functional analyses, the current knowledge of the pig functional genome remains limited (Brown and Moore, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: ENU is a potent mutagen that primarily induces point mutations and chromosome rearrangements in the genome in a random manner.
source: ENU is a potent mutagen that primarily induces point mutations and chromosome rearrangements in the genome in a random manner (Russell et al., 1979).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Russell et al., 1979, establishing the mutagenic properties of ENU.

claim: ENU mutagenesis has advantages over knockout strategies in that it generates a series of point mutations that frequently mimic the subtlety and heterogeneity of human genetic lesions.
source: ENU mutagenesis has advantages over knockout strategies in that it generates a series of point mutations that frequently mimic the subtlety and heterogeneity of human genetic lesions (Oliver and Davies, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Oliver and Davies, 2012.

claim: ENU mutagenesis has been used to generate thousands of mutants in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: In the past, ENU mutagenesis had been used to generate thousands of mutants in Caenorhabditis elegans (De Stasio and Dorman, 2001), flies (Choi et al., 2009; Yu et al., 1987), zebrafish (Driever et al., 1996; Geisler et al., 2007; Haffter et al., 1996; Wienholds et al., 2003; Xiao et al., 2005) and mice (Hrabé de Angelis et al., 2000; Nolan et al., 2000; Vitaterna et al., 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to De Stasio and Dorman, 2001.

claim: ENU mutagenesis has been used to generate mutants in flies.
source: In the past, ENU mutagenesis had been used to generate thousands of mutants in Caenorhabditis elegans (De Stasio and Dorman, 2001), flies (Choi et al., 2009; Yu et al., 1987), zebrafish (Driever et al., 1996; Geisler et al., 2007; Haffter et al., 1996; Wienholds et al., 2003; Xiao et al., 2005) and mice (Hrabé de Angelis et al., 2000; Nolan et al., 2000; Vitaterna et al., 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2009 and Yu et al., 1987.

claim: ENU mutagenesis has been used to generate mutants in zebrafish.
source: In the past, ENU mutagenesis had been used to generate thousands of mutants in Caenorhabditis elegans (De Stasio and Dorman, 2001), flies (Choi et al., 2009; Yu et al., 1987), zebrafish (Driever et al., 1996; Geisler et al., 2007; Haffter et al., 1996; Wienholds et al., 2003; Xiao et al., 2005) and mice (Hrabé de Angelis et al., 2000; Nolan et al., 2000; Vitaterna et al., 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple zebrafish studies.

claim: ENU mutagenesis has been used to generate mutants in mice.
source: In the past, ENU mutagenesis had been used to generate thousands of mutants in Caenorhabditis elegans (De Stasio and Dorman, 2001), flies (Choi et al., 2009; Yu et al., 1987), zebrafish (Driever et al., 1996; Geisler et al., 2007; Haffter et al., 1996; Wienholds et al., 2003; Xiao et al., 2005) and mice (Hrabé de Angelis et al., 2000; Nolan et al., 2000; Vitaterna et al., 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple mouse studies.

claim: The effectiveness of ENU mutagenesis in large mammalian species remains unknown.
source: However, the effectiveness of ENU mutagenesis in large mammalian species remains unknown.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The Bama miniature pig is a southern Chinese native breed with a body weight of 20–30 kg at 6 months of age.
source: The Bama miniature pig, a southern Chinese native breed with a body weight of 20–30 kg at 6 months of age, was used for mutagenesis in the present study.
evidence: This is a factual description of the pig breed used in the study.

claim: ENU was injected at concentrations of 65 or 85 mg/kg bodyweight three times, with a week between injections, into 7- to 8-month-old boars.
source: To determine an appropriate mutagenic but non-toxic dose of ENU (Justice et al., 2000), an ENU concentration of 65 or 85 mg/kg bodyweight was intravenously injected three times, with a week between the injections, into 7- to 8-month-old boars (G0) (Figure 1A) (Hrabé de Angelis et al., 2000).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: The treated boars showed poor-quality sperm at 2–3 weeks after the last injection.
source: The treated boars showed poor-quality sperm at 2–3 weeks after the last injection and underwent a period of azoospermia for 6–8 weeks.
evidence: This observation is supported by sperm quality data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The treated boars underwent a period of azoospermia for 6–8 weeks.
source: The treated boars showed poor-quality sperm at 2–3 weeks after the last injection and underwent a period of azoospermia for 6–8 weeks.
evidence: This observation is supported by sperm quality data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: G0 boars recovered fertility at 12–14 weeks post-treatment.
source: G0 boars recovered fertility at 12–14 weeks post-treatment, and there were no obvious differences in sperm quality between the two treatment groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is supported by sperm quality data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no obvious differences in sperm quality between the 65 mg/kg and 85 mg/kg treatment groups.
source: G0 boars recovered fertility at 12–14 weeks post-treatment, and there were no obvious differences in sperm quality between the two treatment groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ENU treatment predominantly introduced G>A transitions.
source: The results indicated that ENU treatment produced a significant number of G to A transitions, and these transitions occurred far more frequently than did transversions (71.2% for transitions versus 28.8% for transversions) (Figure 1B,C and D).
evidence: This is supported by the mutation spectrum analysis shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Transitions occurred at a frequency of 71.2%, whereas transversions occurred at a frequency of 28.8%.
source: The results indicated that ENU treatment produced a significant number of G to A transitions, and these transitions occurred far more frequently than did transversions (71.2% for transitions versus 28.8% for transversions) (Figure 1B,C and D).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1D.

claim: An increase of mutation frequency in the 85 mg/kg treatment group was observed compared with the 65 mg/kg treatment group (5.86 × 10−6 vs. 1.63 × 10−6).
source: An increase of mutation frequency in the 85 mg/kg treatment group was observed compared with the 65 mg/kg treatment group (5.86 × 10−6 vs. 1.63 × 10−6) (Supplementary file 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary files 1 and 2.

claim: Each G1 pig carried 4,500–16,458 heterozygous mutations throughout the genome.
source: The mutation frequency indicated that each G1 pig carried 4,500–16,458 heterozygous mutations throughout the genome (pig genome size 2.81 × 109 bp), most of which were presumably located in the intergenic area (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is calculated from the mutation frequency data and genome size.

claim: Most ENU-induced mutations were located in the intergenic area.
source: The mutation frequency indicated that each G1 pig carried 4,500–16,458 heterozygous mutations throughout the genome (pig genome size 2.81 × 109 bp), most of which were presumably located in the intergenic area (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E, which displays the distribution of mutations across genomic regions.

claim: A dose of 3 × 85 mg/kg ENU for three treatments is suitable for effective mutagenesis in Bama miniature boars.
source: We concluded that a dose of 3 × 85 mg/kg ENU for three treatments is suitable for effective mutagenesis in Bama miniature boars.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the mutation frequency data and sperm recovery observations.

claim: 36 dominant mutant lines were recovered from the screening of 6,770 G1 offspring, indicating a mutation frequency of ~0.27%.
source: In this pilot study, 36 dominant mutant lines were recovered from the screening of 6,770 G1 offspring, indicating a mutation frequency of ~0.27% (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the screening data presented in Table 1.

claim: Seven mutant pigs were confirmed to have traits that had dominant inheritance (19%, 7/36).
source: Among these offspring, seven mutant pigs were confirmed to have traits that had dominant inheritance (19%, 7/36) (Table 1, Figure 3A–G).
evidence: This is supported by inheritance testing data shown in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: A total of 169 pedigrees produced more than 30 G3 offspring.
source: A total of 169 pedigrees produced more than 30 G3 offspring, and 91 mutant lines were identified, giving a rate of approximately 0.5 mutants (91/169) per pedigree, which is similar to that observed in mice (Hrabé de Angelis et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a direct report of the screening results.

claim: 91 mutant lines were identified from the recessive screen, giving a rate of approximately 0.5 mutants per pedigree.
source: A total of 169 pedigrees produced more than 30 G3 offspring, and 91 mutant lines were identified, giving a rate of approximately 0.5 mutants (91/169) per pedigree, which is similar to that observed in mice (Hrabé de Angelis et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by the screening data and compared to mouse studies.

claim: The mutant recovery rate in pigs is similar to that observed in mice.
source: A total of 169 pedigrees produced more than 30 G3 offspring, and 91 mutant lines were identified, giving a rate of approximately 0.5 mutants (91/169) per pedigree, which is similar to that observed in mice (Hrabé de Angelis et al., 2000).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citation to Hrabé de Angelis et al., 2000.

claim: 22 of the 91 mutant lines were confirmed as inheritable.
source: Among these mutants, 22 of the 91 mutant lines were confirmed as inheritable.
evidence: This is supported by inheritance testing data.

claim: Line Z0009 showed ectropion, flattening of the ears and large, thick, plate-like scales over the entire body, similar to the characteristics of congenital harlequin ichthyosis.
source: The line Z0009 showed ectropion, flattening of the ears and large, thick, plate-like scales over the entire body (Figure 3J), similar to the characteristics of congenital harlequin ichthyosis (OMIM, 242500), and linkage analysis identified its mutant locus at chr15: 120–134 Mb interval.
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic observations shown in Figure 3J and linkage analysis data in Table 2.

claim: Linkage analysis identified the mutant locus of line Z0009 at chr15: 120–134 Mb interval.
source: The line Z0009 showed ectropion, flattening of the ears and large, thick, plate-like scales over the entire body (Figure 3J), similar to the characteristics of congenital harlequin ichthyosis (OMIM, 242500), and linkage analysis identified its mutant locus at chr15: 120–134 Mb interval.
evidence: This is supported by linkage analysis data shown in Table 2.

claim: Lines Z0078 and Z0079 showed abnormal facial and limb development similar to characteristics observed in popliteal pterygium syndrome.
source: Lines Z0078 and Z0079 (Figure 3M), which had a significant linkage signal at chr13: 210–216 Mb, showed abnormal facial and limb development similar to characteristics observed in popliteal pterygium syndrome (OMIM, 263650).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic observations shown in Figure 3M and linkage analysis data in Table 2.

claim: Lines Z0078 and Z0079 had a significant linkage signal at chr13: 210–216 Mb.
source: Lines Z0078 and Z0079 (Figure 3M), which had a significant linkage signal at chr13: 210–216 Mb, showed abnormal facial and limb development similar to characteristics observed in popliteal pterygium syndrome (OMIM, 263650).
evidence: This is supported by linkage analysis data shown in Table 2.

claim: Homozygous mutant pigs of line Z0006 showed a significantly higher body weight at 6 months of age (33.95 ± 7.39 kg vs. 20.04 ± 5.68 kg in wild type pigs, p=3.37E-06).
source: When compared with wild-type pigs, homozygous mutant pigs of line Z0006 showed a significantly higher body weight at 6 months of age (33.95 ± 7.39 kg vs. 20.04 ± 5.68 kg in wild type pigs (WT), p=3.37E-06) and an increase in daily body weight gain (0.23 ± 0.03 kg/d vs. 0.18 ± 0.04 kg/d in WT), phenotypes that were inherited in a recessive manner (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Line Z0006 mutants showed an increase in daily body weight gain (0.23 ± 0.03 kg/d vs. 0.18 ± 0.04 kg/d in WT).
source: When compared with wild-type pigs, homozygous mutant pigs of line Z0006 showed a significantly higher body weight at 6 months of age (33.95 ± 7.39 kg vs. 20.04 ± 5.68 kg in wild type pigs (WT), p=3.37E-06) and an increase in daily body weight gain (0.23 ± 0.03 kg/d vs. 0.18 ± 0.04 kg/d in WT), phenotypes that were inherited in a recessive manner (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate measurements.

claim: The genome-wide association study revealed a strong association between the Z0006 phenotype and the chr6: 122–123 Mb region (p=4.00E-06).
source: The genome-wide association study revealed a strong association between this phenotype and the chr6: 122–123 Mb region (p=4.00E-06).
evidence: This is supported by GWAS data shown in Table 2.

claim: Three strains (Z0139, Z0154 and Z0156) showed decreased body size and weight at 6 months of age (10.60 ± 2.19, 10.02 ± 3.82, 11.94 ± 1.56 vs. 20.99 ± 1.32 in WT all p<0.05).
source: Three other strains (Z0139, Z0154 and Z0156) showed decreased body size and weight at 6 months of age (10.60 ± 2.19, 10.02 ± 3.82, 11.94 ± 1.56 vs. 20.99 ± 1.32 in WT all p<0.05) and could therefore potentially be bred as miniaturized experimental pigs with an adult body weight of less than 10 kg at adulthood.
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The 'Liang-tou-wu' coat color pattern (black coat on the head and bottom and white coat on the body) is a unique pattern in certain Chinese native breeds.
source: The 'Liang-tou-wu' coat color pattern (black coat on the head and bottom and white coat on the body) is a unique pattern in certain Chinese native breeds, and its genetic mechanism remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about pig coat color patterns in Chinese breeds.

claim: The genetic mechanism of the 'Liang-tou-wu' coat color pattern remains unclear.
source: The 'Liang-tou-wu' coat color pattern (black coat on the head and bottom and white coat on the body) is a unique pattern in certain Chinese native breeds, and its genetic mechanism remains unclear.
evidence: This establishes a knowledge gap in pig genetics.

claim: Three mutant pedigrees (Z0017, Z0022 and Z0040) that displayed the 'single-end black' coat color phenotype were derived from different G0 boars.
source: Interestingly, three mutant pedigrees (Z0017, Z0022 and Z0040) that displayed the 'single-end black' coat color phenotype were derived from different G0 boars (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by pedigree information in Table 2.

claim: A mutation in Archain 1 resulted in a diluted coat color and Purkinje cell degeneration.
source: Xu et al. (2010) reported that a mutation in Archain 1 resulted in a diluted coat color and Purkinje cell degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2010.

claim: The occurrence of cutaneous melanoma is strongly associated with mutations in pigmentation-related genes.
source: The occurrence of cutaneous melanoma, a malignant cancer, is strongly associated with mutations in pigmentation-related genes; thus, coat color mutant pigs could be effective models for studying melanomas (Eggermont et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eggermont et al., 2014.

claim: The mutant line TBB007T095 was characterized by white coat color and diluted iris pigmentation, which showed a dominant inheritance pattern (47%, 63/134).
source: The mutant line (TBB007T095) was characterized first by white coat color and diluted iris pigmentation, which showed a dominant inheritance pattern (47%, 63/134) (Figure 3G, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic observations and inheritance data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: All mutants of line TBB007T095 with a white coat color showed profound hearing loss.
source: Our results showed that all mutants with a white coat color showed profound hearing loss, and no peak could be provoked in response to stimulus intensities until 120 dB SPL, whereas wild-type individuals had hearing thresholds of 30–40 dB SPL (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by ABR testing data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Wild-type individuals had hearing thresholds of 30–40 dB SPL.
source: Our results showed that all mutants with a white coat color showed profound hearing loss, and no peak could be provoked in response to stimulus intensities until 120 dB SPL, whereas wild-type individuals had hearing thresholds of 30–40 dB SPL (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by ABR testing data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: GWLS under a dominant model revealed only one genome-wide significant linkage signal (LOD >3) in chromosome 5 (7–71 Mb) for line TBB007T095.
source: GWLS under a dominant model revealed only one genome-wide significant linkage signal (LOD >3) in chromosome 5 (7–71 Mb) (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by linkage analysis data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A missense mutation (c. 325 A>T) in SOX10 resulted in a highly conserved amino acid substitution (R109W).
source: To isolate the causative gene, the hypopigmentation-related gene SOX10 within the linkage region was first selected as a candidate gene, and a missense mutation (c. 325 A>T) that resulted in a highly conserved amino acid substitution (R109W) was identified by sequencing the SOX10 coding sequence (Figure 4B and Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Only the SOX10 R109W mutation completely co-segregated with the hearing-loss phenotype in line TBB007T095.
source: Furthermore, whole-genome sequencing of two independent mutants and one wild-type pig with average read-depth coverages of 11.51×, 10.64×, and 10.63×, respectively, was performed to investigate the mutations in the linkage region. The results indicated that only the SOX10 R109W mutation (SOX10+/R109W), but no other variants, completely co-segregated with the hearing-loss phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The SOX10 c. 325 A>T mutation was not observed in the dbSNP database or in other pig breeds.
source: Furthermore, this mutation was not observed in the dbSNP database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/projects/SNP/) or in other pig breeds (Supplementary file 3), indicating that this mutation was generated by ENU mutagenesis.
evidence: This is supported by database searches and sequencing of other pig breeds.

claim: The SOX10 c. 325 A>T mutation was generated by ENU mutagenesis.
source: Furthermore, this mutation was not observed in the dbSNP database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/projects/SNP/) or in other pig breeds (Supplementary file 3), indicating that this mutation was generated by ENU mutagenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of the mutation in databases and other breeds, combined with the ENU treatment.

claim: The inner ear of the wild-type miniature pig presents several key features that are similar to those of the human ear.
source: The inner ear of the wild-type miniature pig presents several key features that are similar to those of the human ear (Guo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2015.

claim: The mutant miniature pig inner ear has only one and a half cochlea turns.
source: The results showed that the mutant miniature pig inner ear has only one and a half cochlea turns (red arrow in Figure 4E, upper panel), top loop fusing, a short modiolus, and stunted growth, which perfectly mimics the syndrome of human Mondini dysplasia (Figure 4E, upper panel).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis and micro-CT imaging shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The wild-type pig inner ear has three cochlear turns.
source: By contrast, the wild-type pig inner ear has three cochlear turns.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The TBB007T095 mutant perfectly mimics the syndrome of human Mondini dysplasia.
source: The results showed that the mutant miniature pig inner ear has only one and a half cochlea turns (red arrow in Figure 4E, upper panel), top loop fusing, a short modiolus, and stunted growth, which perfectly mimics the syndrome of human Mondini dysplasia (Figure 4E, upper panel).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the mutant phenotype with human Mondini dysplasia characteristics.

claim: SOX10 might be responsible for human Mondini dysplasia.
source: These data suggest that SOX10 might be responsible for human Mondini dysplasia, and this strain represents the first inherited animal model of human dysplasia.
evidence: This is inferred from the pig model data showing SOX10 mutation causes Mondini-like phenotype.

claim: The TBB007T095 strain represents the first inherited animal model of human Mondini dysplasia.
source: These data suggest that SOX10 might be responsible for human Mondini dysplasia, and this strain represents the first inherited animal model of human dysplasia.
evidence: This is based on the lack of previous animal models and the phenotypic similarity to human disease.

claim: Congenital splay leg syndrome is a major cause of lameness in newborn piglets.
source: Congenital splay leg syndrome is a major cause of lameness in newborn piglets and occurs at highly varying frequencies (Dobson, 1968).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dobson, 1968.

claim: The etiology and pathogenetic mechanisms of congenital splay leg syndrome are poorly understood.
source: The etiology and pathogenetic mechanisms of this disease are poorly understood (Maak et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maak et al., 2009.

claim: Mutants of the Z0075 line exhibited hind-limb paralysis with a recessive inheritance pattern (33%, 9/27).
source: Mutants of the Z0075 line exhibited hind-limb paralysis with a recessive inheritance pattern (33%, 9/27) (Figure 5A), with muscle atrophy and interstitial fibrosis in the hind limb skeletal muscles (semitendinosus) and longissimus dorsi but not in the fore-limb muscles (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic observations and inheritance data shown in Figure 5A and Table 2.

claim: Z0075 mutants showed muscle atrophy and interstitial fibrosis in the hind limb skeletal muscles but not in the fore-limb muscles.
source: Mutants of the Z0075 line exhibited hind-limb paralysis with a recessive inheritance pattern (33%, 9/27) (Figure 5A), with muscle atrophy and interstitial fibrosis in the hind limb skeletal muscles (semitendinosus) and longissimus dorsi but not in the fore-limb muscles (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Genetic mapping results for Z0075 showed the strongest linkage signal at the chr4: 16–17 Mb region.
source: Genetic mapping results showed the strongest linkage signal at the chr4: 16–17 Mb region, within which 20 genes with certain function are found (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by linkage analysis data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: 20 genes with certain function are found within the chr4: 16–17 Mb region.
source: Genetic mapping results showed the strongest linkage signal at the chr4: 16–17 Mb region, within which 20 genes with certain function are found (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation data in Supplementary file 4.

claim: FBXO32 is located in the chr4: 16–17 Mb region and was previously identified as a skeletal muscle atrophy related gene.
source: Interestingly, FBXO32, previously identified as a skeletal muscle atrophy related gene, is located in this region.
evidence: This is based on gene location data and established knowledge about FBXO32 function.

claim: FBXO32 was highly expressed in the skeletal muscles in the Z0075 affected animals at both the transcriptional and protein levels.
source: Although the disease-causing mutation has not yet been located in the sequences of these genes, expression analysis indicated that FBXO32 was highly expressed in the skeletal muscles in the affected animals at both the transcriptional and protein levels (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: The expression of MyoD and MyoG was downregulated in the skeletal muscles of Z0075 mutants.
source: The expression of MyoD and MyoG, the master regulators of skeletal myogenesis, which drives the differentiation of myoblasts into multinucleated myotubes (Rudnicki et al., 1993), was downregulated in the skeletal muscles, whereas expression of another main regulator, MYF5, remained unchanged in these mutants, suggesting the potential negative regulation of MyoD and MyoG by FBXO32 (Tintignac et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Expression of MYF5 remained unchanged in Z0075 mutants.
source: The expression of MyoD and MyoG, the master regulators of skeletal myogenesis, which drives the differentiation of myoblasts into multinucleated myotubes (Rudnicki et al., 1993), was downregulated in the skeletal muscles, whereas expression of another main regulator, MYF5, remained unchanged in these mutants, suggesting the potential negative regulation of MyoD and MyoG by FBXO32 (Tintignac et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: FBXO32 potentially negatively regulates MyoD and MyoG.
source: The expression of MyoD and MyoG, the master regulators of skeletal myogenesis, which drives the differentiation of myoblasts into multinucleated myotubes (Rudnicki et al., 1993), was downregulated in the skeletal muscles, whereas expression of another main regulator, MYF5, remained unchanged in these mutants, suggesting the potential negative regulation of MyoD and MyoG by FBXO32 (Tintignac et al., 2005).
evidence: This is inferred from the expression data and supported by citation to Tintignac et al., 2005.

claim: MyoD and MyoG are master regulators of skeletal myogenesis that drive the differentiation of myoblasts into multinucleated myotubes.
source: The expression of MyoD and MyoG, the master regulators of skeletal myogenesis, which drives the differentiation of myoblasts into multinucleated myotubes (Rudnicki et al., 1993), was downregulated in the skeletal muscles
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rudnicki et al., 1993.

claim: The drawbacks of conventional model organisms have hindered the direct applicability of model-obtained knowledge to human therapies.
source: Indeed, the drawbacks of the conventional model organisms have hindered the direct applicability of model-obtained knowledge to human therapies, and the translation of preclinical studies in rodents to clinical trials in humans is frequently unsuccessful (Abarbanell et al., 2010; Wall and Shani, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Abarbanell et al., 2010 and Wall and Shani, 2008.

claim: The translation of preclinical studies in rodents to clinical trials in humans is frequently unsuccessful.
source: Indeed, the drawbacks of the conventional model organisms have hindered the direct applicability of model-obtained knowledge to human therapies, and the translation of preclinical studies in rodents to clinical trials in humans is frequently unsuccessful (Abarbanell et al., 2010; Wall and Shani, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Abarbanell et al., 2010 and Wall and Shani, 2008.

claim: Pigs could be used as alternatives to dogs or monkeys as the non-rodent species in preclinical toxicological testing of pharmaceuticals.
source: Pigs could be used as alternatives to dogs or monkeys as the non-rodent species in preclinical toxicological testing of pharmaceuticals (Swindle et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Swindle et al., 2012.

claim: Over the past two decades, pigs replaced dogs as surgical models in the international arena for both training and research.
source: Over the past two decades, pigs also replaced dogs as surgical models in the international arena for both training and research.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical trend in surgical model use.

claim: The progress of pig genomics and functional genomics is lagging behind in health research.
source: However, the progress of pig genomics and functional genomics is lagging behind in health research.
evidence: This establishes a knowledge gap in pig genomics.

claim: The swine genome sequence is on version 10.2, whereas the human and mouse genomes are on versions 37 and 38, respectively.
source: For example, the swine genome sequence is on version 10.2, whereas the human and mouse genomes are on versions 37 and 38, respectively (Prather, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prather, 2013.

claim: ENU produces not only null alleles but also hypomorphs and gain of function mutations.
source: As a point mutagen, ENU produces not only null alleles but also hypomorphs and gain of function mutations, which are more similar to many mutations associated with human diseases (Wilson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2005.

claim: Hypomorphic phenotypes or partial loss of function can be significantly different from the null phenotype normally produced by knockout approaches.
source: Hypomorphic phenotypes or partial loss of function can be significantly different from the null phenotype normally produced by knockout approaches and can provide information on the function of genes in developmental or pathological processes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about different types of mutations.

claim: Dosing with three injections of 85 mg/kg at 1 week intervals is effective to introduce mutations in the pig genome at a frequency (5.86 × 10−6) similar to that observed in mice.
source: As there is no reference that describes optimized ENU mutagenesis in pigs, we optimized the ENU treatment protocol in pigs and observed that dosing with three injections of 85 mg/kg at 1 week intervals is effective to introduce mutations in the pig genome at a frequency (5.86 × 10−6) similar to that observed in mice (Concepcion et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by mutation frequency data and comparison to mouse studies.

claim: The average rate of de novo mutation is approximately 1.2 × 10−8 mutations per site per generation in humans.
source: The average rate of de novo mutation is approximately 1.2 × 10−8 mutations per site per generation in humans (Kong et al., 2012; Roach et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kong et al., 2012 and Roach et al., 2010.

claim: ENU can significantly increase the mutation rate by 130–480-fold in pigs when using the current protocol.
source: Thus, the results of the present study indicated that ENU can significantly increase the mutation rate by 130–480-fold in pigs when using the current protocol.
evidence: This is calculated from the comparison of ENU-induced mutation rate to natural mutation rate.

claim: Around 4,580–16,466 ENU-induced mutations could be identified per G1 pig across the whole genome.
source: Taking the predicted coding sequence size of the pig genome, around 4,580–16,466 ENU-induced mutations could be identified per G1 pig across the whole genome, and around 57–205 variants might occur in the coding regions.
evidence: This is calculated from the mutation frequency and genome size.

claim: Around 57–205 variants might occur in the coding regions per G1 pig.
source: Taking the predicted coding sequence size of the pig genome, around 4,580–16,466 ENU-induced mutations could be identified per G1 pig across the whole genome, and around 57–205 variants might occur in the coding regions.
evidence: This is calculated from the mutation frequency and coding sequence size.

claim: Approximately 55% of the ENU-induced mutations in coding sequences result in amino acid changes in mice.
source: Based on ENU mutagenesis in mice, assuming that ~55% of the ENU-induced mutations in coding sequences result in amino acid changes (Quwailid et al., 2004), approximately 31–113 functional mutations might be detected in each G1 pig.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Quwailid et al., 2004.

claim: Approximately 31–113 functional mutations might be detected in each G1 pig.
source: Based on ENU mutagenesis in mice, assuming that ~55% of the ENU-induced mutations in coding sequences result in amino acid changes (Quwailid et al., 2004), approximately 31–113 functional mutations might be detected in each G1 pig.
evidence: This is calculated from the number of coding variants and the proportion that cause amino acid changes.

claim: Approximately 710 G1 pigs are required to identify one functional mutation in a specific gene from the pig genome.
source: Approximately 710 G1 pigs are required to identify one functional mutation in a specific gene from the pig genome (the number of coding genes in pig is ~2.2 × 104, and the average length of the coding DNA sequence (CDS) of a gene is 1.6 × 103 bp).
evidence: This is calculated from the number of genes and mutation frequency.

claim: In mice, the optimal dose produces approximately one mutation with phenotypic effects per gene per 700–1000 gametes.
source: In mice, the optimal dose produces approximately one mutation with phenotypic effects per gene per 700–1000 gametes (Hitotsumachi et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hitotsumachi et al., 1985.

claim: It is feasible to establish gene-driven mutagenesis by archiving sufficient DNA and sperm from G1 pigs.
source: Therefore, it is feasible to establish gene-driven mutagenesis by archiving sufficient DNA and sperm from G1 pigs.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutation frequency calculations and comparison to mouse studies.

claim: One of the major rate-limiting steps in ENU mutagenesis is the identification of individual causative mutations.
source: One of the major rate-limiting steps in ENU mutagenesis is the identification of individual causative mutations (Hrabé de Angelis et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hrabé de Angelis et al., 2000.

claim: With the rapidly decreasing cost of whole-genome sequencing, all G3 ENU pigs can be sequenced at a depth sufficient to identify and segregate all of the mutations for linkage analysis.
source: However, with the rapidly decreasing cost of whole-genome sequencing, all G3 ENU pigs can be sequenced at a depth sufficient to identify and segregate all of the mutations for linkage analysis (Bull et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bull et al., 2013 and current sequencing technology capabilities.

claim: Hearing loss is the most common sensory disorder.
source: Hearing loss is the most common sensory disorder, and congenital genetic deafness has an incidence of 1 in 1,600 children (Iizuka et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iizuka et al., 2015.

claim: Congenital genetic deafness has an incidence of 1 in 1,600 children.
source: Hearing loss is the most common sensory disorder, and congenital genetic deafness has an incidence of 1 in 1,600 children (Iizuka et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iizuka et al., 2015.

claim: Animal models of human genetic deafness play a central role in the exploration and development of new therapies.
source: Animal models of human genetic deafness play a central role in the exploration and development of new therapies (Vodicka et al., 2005), but rodent models cannot satisfy the demand due to the smaller size of their cochlear organs and the physiology of rodent hearing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vodicka et al., 2005.

claim: Rodent models cannot satisfy the demand for hearing loss research due to the smaller size of their cochlear organs and the physiology of rodent hearing.
source: Animal models of human genetic deafness play a central role in the exploration and development of new therapies (Vodicka et al., 2005), but rodent models cannot satisfy the demand due to the smaller size of their cochlear organs and the physiology of rodent hearing.
evidence: This is based on anatomical and physiological differences between rodents and humans.

claim: Human hearing and hearing in pigs have many physiological similarities.
source: However, human hearing and hearing in pigs have many physiological similarities, and the breeding and handling advantages of pigs make pigs the most suitable animal model for clinical otological and audiological studies.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about pig and human auditory systems.

claim: Mondini dysplasia occurs at a rate of 0.5–1/1000 in children.
source: Mondini dysplasia occurs at a rate of 0.5–1/1000 in children and can be identified in various syndromes (Deenadayal et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deenadayal et al., 2010.

claim: The major pathologies of Mondini dysplasia are cochlear malformation with dilatation of the vestibule, aqueduct, and ampulla and the incomplete partitioning of the cochlea.
source: The major pathologies of Mondini dysplasia are cochlear malformation with dilatation of the vestibule, aqueduct, and ampulla and the incomplete partitioning of the cochlea (Zheng et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2002.

claim: The genetic mechanism and inheritance pattern of Mondini dysplasia are unknown.
source: The genetic mechanism and inheritance pattern of Mondini dysplasia are unknown, and no human inheritance family or animal model has been reported.
evidence: This establishes a knowledge gap in understanding Mondini dysplasia.

claim: No human inheritance family or animal model of Mondini dysplasia has been reported.
source: The genetic mechanism and inheritance pattern of Mondini dysplasia are unknown, and no human inheritance family or animal model has been reported.
evidence: This establishes the novelty of the pig model described in the study.

claim: A large number of quantitative trait loci (QTL) have been mapped for a wide range of economically important traits in pigs.
source: A large number of quantitative trait loci (QTL) have been mapped for a wide range of economically important traits in pigs (Ernst and Steibel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ernst and Steibel, 2013.

claim: Only limited numbers of QTL were mapped to defined quantitative trait genes (QTGs) and quantitative trait nucleotides (QTNs).
source: However, only limited numbers of QTL were mapped to defined quantitative trait genes (QTGs) and quantitative trait nucleotides (QTNs), which can be used for direct selection in pig breeding.
evidence: This establishes a knowledge gap in pig genetics.

claim: Splay leg is the most frequently observed hereditary disorder in newborn piglets, with prevalence ranging from less than 1% to greater than 8% in certain farms.
source: Splay leg is the most frequently observed hereditary disorder in newborn piglets, with prevalence ranging from less than 1% to greater than 8% in certain farms (Partlow et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Partlow et al., 1993.

claim: The affected piglets with splay leg are characterized by an impaired ability to stand and walk, resulting from a muscular weakness of the hind limbs.
source: The affected piglets are characterized by an impaired ability to stand and walk, resulting from a muscular weakness of the hind limbs (Thurley et al., 1967).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thurley et al., 1967.

claim: More than 50% of affected piglets with splay leg will die.
source: More than 50% of affected piglets will die, making congenital splay leg a source of considerable economic losses in pig production (Dobson, 1968).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dobson, 1968.

claim: The role of FBXO32 in pig congenital splay leg syndrome is controversial.
source: Atrophy marker FBXO32 is one of the putative causative genes and showed increased expression in the skeletal muscles of affected piglets (Ooi et al., 2006), but the role of FBXO32 in pig congenital splay leg syndrome is neverthless controversial (Boettcher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ooi et al., 2006 and Boettcher et al., 2008.

claim: Maak et al. (2009) couldn't confirm the role of FBXO32 in pig muscle atrophy.
source: Maak et al. (2009) couldn't confirm the role of FBXO32 in pig muscle atrophy and observed a large individual variability in FBXO32 expression in the skeletal muscles of splay-leg piglets, which has also been described previously (Björklund et al., 1987; Boettcher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maak et al., 2009.

claim: Large individual variability in FBXO32 expression has been observed in the skeletal muscles of splay-leg piglets.
source: Maak et al. (2009) couldn't confirm the role of FBXO32 in pig muscle atrophy and observed a large individual variability in FBXO32 expression in the skeletal muscles of splay-leg piglets, which has also been described previously (Björklund et al., 1987; Boettcher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Björklund et al., 1987 and Boettcher et al., 2008.

claim: This study provides more evidence that FBXO32 might be responsible for congenital splay-leg syndrome in pigs.
source: Therefore, we provided more evidence that FBXO32 might be responsible for congenital splay-leg syndrome in pigs, thereby enhancing the current understanding of the molecular mechanisms regulating pig muscle atrophy and remolding.
evidence: This is based on the expression data from the Z0075 mutant line.

claim: This study demonstrates the feasibility of artificial random mutagenesis in pigs.
source: This study demonstrates the feasibility of artificial random mutagenesis in pigs and opens an avenue for generating a reservoir of mutants for agricultural production and biomedical research.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental results.

claim: ENU mutagenesis in pigs opens an avenue for generating a reservoir of mutants for agricultural production and biomedical research.
source: This study demonstrates the feasibility of artificial random mutagenesis in pigs and opens an avenue for generating a reservoir of mutants for agricultural production and biomedical research.
evidence: This is the main implication of the study based on the successful generation of diverse mutants.

claim: Genome-wide ENU mutagenesis and subsequent phenotypic screening can be used to generate pig mutants with a broad range of phenotypes.
source: The data obtained in the present study showed that genome-wide ENU mutagenesis and subsequent phenotypic screening can be used to generate pig mutants with a broad range of phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by the diverse phenotypes identified in the screening, as shown in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: In combination with gene-targeting strategies, ENU mutagenesis will continue to play an important role in the identification and characterization of mutations that underlie human diseases and pig economic traits.
source: In combination with gene-targeting strategies, ENU mutagenesis will continue to play an important role in the identification and characterization of mutations that underlie human diseases and pig economic traits.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about the future applications of the technology.

claim: The importance of pigs as a biomedical model will further increase in the near future.
source: Based on the results of the present study, the importance of pigs as a biomedical model will further increase in the near future.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the successful demonstration of ENU mutagenesis in pigs.
